Countess Cathleen

Like others I had assumed this to be a Bill Whelan composition. I am now informed that it is not. It seems likely that he added the ‘fill’ after the second part, necessitating a 6/8 bar at the end. The major key third part I think is Whelan’s. Can anyone confirm this? I want to use it for a dance arrangement and don’t want to get into trouble with copyright.

The Countess Cathleen, X:2

The middle section of Countess Cathleen before it transitions to Women of the Sidhe- on the official Riverdance recording, the original Countess Cathleen setting is played through twice before the tune modulates to D maj and this setting is played once. Then the original setting is played through a third and final time.

↳ Posted by gabriellen on June 26th, 2020.

Re: The Countess Cathleen

If it’s not by Bill Whelan, then where is it from? These tunes bear all the hallmarks of a Whelan composition; i.e., rooted in trad but full of funky syncopated bars & higher-octave sections…

I once owned the Riverdance music book, like 22 years ago, but have no idea what happened to it over time (crazy stupid, I know). I do remember every composition in the show being credited to Bill Whelan. He even wrote an introduction in the book as well, explaining his inspiration, style, etc. There are also a lot of valuable side notes & snippets of info included on each piece. I may have to purchase that book again; if you like that music, it’s very helpful to have.

For The Countess Cathleen, on fiddle, the middle tune in D (D2 d cBA GFG…) is often easier to play down an octave. Or you can start in third position on the A string (d2 d‘ c’ba gfg…) and slide back into first on (A2 A def gab…).

I’ve noticed on other tunes from the show, like ‘Slip Into Spring’, Eileen Ivers didn’t shift to 3rd position on the higher octave B-part (fg abc‘ d’dd’ dc’b…), but rather played those few phrases in the middle octave. So there are lots of options if you want to make these pieces easier! But the high Ds and Cs (of the main E minor slip jig) I think should be played the way they’re written! No substitute, really.

↳ Posted by Erik-Fiddler on March 14th, 2024.
